Narrator's Father
The Narrator's Father is the father of the Narrator, making the Narrator a son of a man who owns the family trade. The Narrator demonstrated concern for his father's finances, wishing to spend some of his own means to help him, which led him to choose Mr. Young's place. He also wrote a letter to his father at Brampton and was troubled at not having heard back since leaving him.

The two had numerous personal encounters. The Narrator's Father dined at the Narrator's house with Cousin Scott; on another occasion he came to the Narrator's home and announced his intention to go into the country the next day. The Narrator went to his father's house, and later the father went with him to the Bear Tavern, an alehouse. They also met by appointment at Uncle Fenner's house. After the theatre, the Narrator and his wife went to the Narrator's Father's house and stayed to talk for a while.

In practical matters, the Narrator and his father together decided on scarlet, purple, and black cloth as well as £50 in linen. The Narrator argued with his father over Pall and, after bringing down Pall's high spirit, got his father to yield. He also obtained his father's consent for Pall to go into the country with the Narrator's mother and father, to see how Pall would behave. Additionally, together with Tom, the Narrator and his father set matters even and cast up the father's accounts, reflecting their shared involvement in financial and domestic affairs.

Narrator
The relation between My Lord and the Narrator is one of patronage, trust, and delegated responsibility, centered on the business of the Wardrobe. Before going to sea, My Lord instructed the Narrator in Wardrobe affairs and told him he placed great confidence in him. My Lord also said that the Narrator was to go to Mr. Townsend to learn the mystery of the Wardrobe, and he intended to make the Narrator deputy with Mr. Townsend, given the possibility that Mr. Townsend might die during My Lord’s absence.

The Narrator, in turn, sought and received preferment. He asked My Lord for the refusal of Mr. Young’s place in the Wardrobe should it fall, and My Lord freely promised him the refusal. The Narrator went to My Lord’s residence at Whitehall; on his second visit, he found and spoke with My Lord. On another occasion, by My Lord’s order, My Lord’s triangle virginall was sent to the Narrator’s own house. When My Lord was absent, he sent for the Narrator and entrusted him with seeing all things done concerning the great preparation. The Narrator also spoke at the Tower for ammunition for ships that were for My Lord, wrote to My Lord to report what had been done about the goods, and had letters for My Lord that were not ready when Captain Isham called for them.

The relation (Narrator, Narrator’s Wife) describes the married couple in the diary entries, identifying Narrator’s Wife as the wife of the Narrator and the Narrator as her husband; he consistently refers to her as his wife throughout the diary. Their shared activities include walking together on the leads and then going to bed, dining at home and attending church together on the Lord’s day, and going together to The Theatre and later to the Narrator’s Father’s house.

In everyday matters, the Narrator gave Narrator’s Wife L4 to spend on lace and other things. She also relayed news to him, telling him that Sir W. Pen’s daughter was a plain girl rather than the expected great beauty, and informing him about Balty’s condition and asking the Narrator to do something for Balty.

A note on her health states that she was not sick but out of order, and a faced white coat was made from one of her petticoats.

Mr. Moore and The Narrator were acquainted through a series of social, professional, and informational exchanges. The Narrator once stayed late at the Wardrobe and then went to bed with Mr. Moore in Mr. Moore's chamber. In a legal matter, Mr. Moore sent advice that the three witnesses being legatees would not harm the will. At Whitehall, Mr. Moore read over all the bills in The Narrator's presence, and he also told The Narrator there that Lady Sandwich had given birth to a daughter.
